# Singly-Reduced Iridium Chromophores: Synthesis, Characterization, and Photochemistry

# Yunjung Baek, Adam Reinhold, Lei Tian, Philip D. Jeffrey, Gregory D. Scholes*, and Robert R. Knowles*

Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, United States

ABSTRACT: One-electron reduced photosensitizers have been invoked as crucial intermediates in photoredox catalysis, including multiphoton excitation and electrophotocatalytic processes. However, such a reduced chromophore has been less investigated, limiting mechanistic studies of their associated electron transfer processes. Here, we report the total 11 different examples of isolable singly-reduced iridium chromophores. Chemical reduction of a cyclometalated iridium complex with potassium graphite affords a 19-electron species. Structural and spectroscopic characterization reveals a ligand-centered reduction product. The reduced chromophore absorbs a wide range of light from ultraviolet to near-infrared and exhibits photoinduced bimolecular electron transfer reactivity. These studies shed light on elusive reduced iridium chromophores in both ground and excited states, providing opportunities to investigate a commonly invoked intermediate in photoredox catalysis.

1. INTRODUCTION In recent years, photoredox catalysis has received significant attention as a strategy to generate high-energy intermediates, drive endergonic transformations, or expand the scope of traditional catalytic methods.1, 2 Accordingly, numerous chromophores have been designed and employed in chemical transformations to facilitate the conversion of photons into chemical potential. Among those, cyclometalated Ru(II) and Ir(III)-based photosensitizers (PS) have served as the major development platforms for photoredox catalysts (e.g., [Ru(bpy)3][PF6]2 and Ir(ppy)3).3 Such a lowspin 4d6 or 5d6 metal complex absorbs visible light to undergo a metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) followed by intersystem crossing (ISC), affording a long-lived triplet excited state (3MLCT). This lowest-energy excited state exhibits enhanced oxidizing and reducing powers relative to its ground state (S0), enabling redox transformations that would otherwise not be possible. As such, when the excited photosensitizer (*PS) oxidizes a substrate (e.g., reductive quenching), the corresponding one-electron reduced photocatalyst (PS•–) is formed (Figure 1A).1 The resulting singly-reduced photocatalyst (PS•–) is an essential intermediate in photoredox catalysis. It is commonly proposed to engage in forward electron transfer (ET) steps to furnish a target product. Alternatively, it can participate in charge recombination with an oxidized substrate to return to its ground state (Figure 1A). Furthermore, a monoreduced chromophore has been proposed as a second photon absorber to afford another excited state (*PS•–) or a solvated electron, both of which are exceptionally reducing (Figure 1A).4, 5 Seminal examples from the König and Nicewicz groups have demonstrated that one-electron reduced photosensitizers are competent for photoinduced bimolecular ET using perylene diimide (PDI) and acridinium (Acr) derivatives, respectively (Figure 1B).6 In these studies, the

corresponding one-electron reduced organic chromophore (PS•– = PDI•– or Acr•) was generated photochemically in the presence of an excess amount of a sacrificial electron donor. While direct isolation of the reduced intermediates (e.g., = PDI•– and Acr•) was not reported, these representative examples showcased for the first time that the super-reducing power of the (*PS•–) is capable of cleaving strong bonds. Similarly, electrophotocatalytic processes have been developed to afford (*PS•–) via electrochemical reduction followed by photoexcitation utilizing dicyanoanthracene (DCA) or naphthalene monoimide (NMI) derivatives (Figure 1B).7 In addition to these organic chromophores, an analogous Ir-based reduced photoredox catalyst (PS•–) has been proposed as a viable species for consecutive bimolecular ET (Figure 1B).8 Despite the substantial advances in the field, such singly-reduced photocatalysts (PS•–) are considered to be highly reactive transient intermediates that can be detected only spectroscopically.6, 9 Indeed, in the case of NMI, the corresponding one-electron reduced radical intermediate (e.g., NMI•–) converts into another singlet species (e.g., [NMI(H)–

]), which is chemically different from the parent photocatalyst. Furthermore, while *NMI•– exhibits an extremely short lifetime (e.g., 24 ps), *[NMI(H)–] manifests a 20 ns lifetime along with a strong enough reducing power to activate chloroarenes. These observations suggest that *[NMI(H)–], rather than *NMI•– may be operative during the electrophotocatalysis. As these reports demonstrate, establishing the ET capability of *PS•– remains challenging. For that, the direct isolation of such a reduced intermediate becomes necessary to study its chemical nature both in the ground and excited states.  So far, however, only a small number have been successfully isolated using iron- and zirconium-based photoredox catalysts, as reported by the Wärnmark and Milsmann groups,

respectively.10, 11 The direct isolation of singly-reduced photocatalysts will enable quantification of their concentrations, investigation of their structures and chemical

reactivity, and thus, in-depth mechanistic studies of photoredox processes. Here, we present the independent synthesis of a series of one-electron reduced,

heteroleptic Ir chromophores to disclose their (1) structural identities, (2) ground state electronic configuration, (3) photoinduced reactivities, and (4) photophysical properties. A total of 11 different mono-reduced Ir photoredox catalysts with systematically modified ligands were isolated and crystallographically characterized. Furthermore, their ground and excited state properties have been examined using multi-nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), UV/vis/NIR absorption, and femtosecond time-resolved transient absorption (TA) spectroscopies along with computational analysis.

2. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 2.1. Synthesis and isolation of a reduced Ir chromophore. In targeting the isolation of one-electron reduced Ir chromophores, we envisioned the stoichiometric chemical reduction of a cationic Ir(III) photoredox catalyst in its ground state. Under dinitrogen (N2) atmosphere, treatment of [Ir(dFCF3ppy)2(bpy)][PF6] (1) with a stoichiometric amount of potassium graphite (KC8) in a thawing benzene solution afforded a dark orange reaction mixture. The mixture was filtered through Celite to remove byproducts such as graphite and KPF6. The resulting filtrate was lyophilized to afford the orange powders (Scheme 1).

Scheme 1. Stoichiometric chemical reduction of 1.

Product (2) showed a loss of the diagnostic doublet resonance of hexafluorophosphate ion in its 19F NMR spectrum and the formation of broad chemical resonances judged by 1H NMR spectroscopy. (Figure 2A and Figure S-8). While all of these resonances were observed within a diamagnetic chemical window, their temperature-dependent behavior was confirmed via variable-temperature (VT) 1H NMR spectroscopy to suggest the paramagnetic nature of 2 (Figure 2A). Additionally, treating 2 with one equivalent of ferrocenium hexafluorophosphate (FcPF6) recovered 1H and 19F NMR spectra of 1, accompanying an immediate color change from dark orange to pale yellow (SI-59).

These results led us to assign 2 as the target, one-electron reduced species of 1.

2.2. Physical and electronic structure of 2. The EPR spectrum of 2 in toluene at room temperature revealed an isotropic signal suggesting an open-shell S = ½ ground state (Figure 2B). Interestingly, the solid-state EPR spectrum of 2 in frozen toluene at 10 K exhibited an axial resonance indicating asymmetry in the molecular structure, and thus, spin distribution (Figure 2C). The absence of typical hyperfine structure for a low-spin Ir(II) (d7, S = ½) ion suggests a ligand-centered rather than a metal-based reduction. Collectively, the results suggest that 2 is a neutral, paramagnetic compound corresponding to the one-electron reduced form of 1 (Scheme 1). To further establish the chemical identity of 2, single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction were grown from a 1:1 benzene/hexane mixture at room temperature and compared to the crystal structure of 1 (Figure 3A – D). In line with the aforementioned multi-nuclear NMR assignments, the solid-state structure of 2 confirmed the absence of a hexafluorophosphate ion to support the compound’s neutral charge (Figure 3B). The obtained solid-state structure revealed apparent changes in bond distances of the Irbound bpy ligand. In contrast to 1, 2 exhibits a substantially shortened bond distance of C2–C2’ (1.479(3) → 1.423(3) Å), while the four adjacent C–C bonds are elongated (Figure 3C and 3D). Consequently, the rest of the bonds display an alternating pattern of contraction and elongation (Figure 3D).

These bond length changes of the bpy ligand of 2 are characteristic of a bpy radical anion (bpy•–) bound to an alkali metal (e.g., Na or K) or transition metal ion.12 Additionally, 2 exhibits distinctive UV/vis/NIR absorptions resulting from the unique π*–π* transitions of a (bpy•–) moiety (Figure 3E). The absorption spectrum of 2 in benzene exhibits a strong UV absorbance, medium intensity visible light absorption, and relatively weak NIR transitions. The vibronic coupling features of visible light and NIR absorptions are comparable to those of a metal-free bpy•– measured spectroelectrochemically.13, 14 These results suggest that the molecular orbitals (MOs) of 2 involved in the visible light and NIR transitions are heavily (bpy•–)-based. The foregoing spectroscopic and crystallographic data are further corroborated by DFT calculations.15 The singly-occupied molecular orbital (SOMO) of geometry-optimized 2 is mostly localized on the Ir-bound bpy ligand (Figure 3F). In particular, the pattern of bonding or antibonding interaction illustrated in the SOMO matches with the bond length changes in the solid-state structure of 2. Considering that the lowest-energy unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of 1 is a neutral bpy-based π* orbital that is participating in MLCT, the analysis agrees that the LUMO becomes the SOMO of 2 upon the reduction. Taken all together, 2 can be best described as a neutral IrIII(dFCF3ppy)2(bpy•–) complex with the ground state electronic configuration of (5d6 + bpy•–, 19e‒, S = ½).

The foregoing observations led us to examine the effect of the substitution pattern (e.g., C4 vs. C5) on the chemical properties of a reduced Ir chromophore. To this end, a 5,5’-dCF3 substituted congener (7) was synthesized given its wide use in photoredox catalysis (Scheme 2). Surprisingly, while its regioisomer 6 is yellow in solution, a benzene solution of 7 is red (Figure 4B). The difference suggests that the substitution pattern influences the energy gap between the frontier molecular orbitals (FMOs) for visible light-induced π*– π* transitions.

2.4. Variation of the ppy ligand. The structural, spectroscopic, and theoretical characterization of 2 – 7 collectively support that the SOMO of a reduced Ir chromophore is localized on the bpy ligand in all cases. As a result, the absorption spectra of 2 – 7 in the visible and NIR regions resemble the characteristic π*–π* transitions of a parent (bpy•–) (Figure 4).14 However, unlike the π*–π* transitions of a metal-free (bpy•–), those transitions for 2 – 7 could be affected by the additional π* orbitals of the ppy ligands. Specifically, as the energies for the π* MOs of the ppy ligand are close to that of the SOMO, the ppy-based π* MOs could participate in the π*–π* transitions as an acceptor MO. In other words, the identity of the electron-accepting π* MO for these π*–π* transitions remains elusive.

To investigate the nature of the acceptor π* MO or the involvement of the ppy ligands in the π*–π* transitions, a second chemical series of the reduced Ir chromophores was prepared. We selected a family of the widely utilized, commercially available heteroleptic Ir photoredox catalysts possessing various ppy ligands. The identity of the bpy ligand (e.g., 4,4’-d(tBu)bpy) was retained across the series, but the electron-withdrawing substituents (e.g., F, CF3) on the ppy ligands were replaced with an H-atom or methyl group to cover a wide range of redox potentials (Scheme 3). The same synthetic route utilizing stoichiometric KC8 provided access to the four additional reduced chromophores, 8 – 11 (Scheme 3). Multi-nuclear NMR, EPR, and UV/vis/NIR absorption spectroscopies along with singlecrystal X-ray diffraction and DFT studies were carried out for 8 – 11. As in the bpy-chemical series (2 – 7), the ground state electronic configuration of 8 – 11 is assigned as (5d6 + (bpy•–), 19e‒, S = ½). However, in contrast to the bpy-chemical series (2 – 7), compounds 4 and 8 – 11 revealed almost the identical absorption spectra in terms of their absorption energies and molar absorptivity in both the visible and NIR regions (Figure 6A). These results suggest that the contribution of the ppy ligands to the π*–π* transitions are negligible, and therefore, the nature of both the donor and acceptor π* MOs are mostly bpy-based. As shown in Figures 6B and 6C, EPR spectra of 4 and 8 – 11 in toluene at room temperature exhibit similar g-factors,

whereas the g values for 2 – 6 were varied to a greater extent. Deviation from the expected g factor (ge = 2.003) in all cases (2 – 11) is likely due to a non-zero contribution of a metal ion as illustrated in their SOMOs. Nonetheless, these results imply that the g factor is mostly dictated by the identity of a reduced bpy ligand. In other words, the aforementioned data collectively support that the ground state

electronic configuration of 2 – 11 can be best illustrated as Figure 6D, where a formally Ir(III) center is bound to the singly-reduced bpy ligand (5d6 + (bpy•–), 19e‒, S = ½) to engender an overall neutral, paramagnetic species (Figure S- 127).

2.5. Variation of the nature of SOMO. Thus far, we have confirmed the ground state electronic structure of a family of mono-reduced Ir chromophores. Our characterization data supports that their spectroscopic properties were the result of a bpy ligand with a localized SOMO (Figure 6D). Intrigued by these results, we next sought to alter the chemical identity of SOMO to a greater extent by replacing the bpy with a phenanthroline ligand. To this end, chemical reduction of a 1,10-phenanthrolinebound congener (e.g., [Ir(dFCF3ppy)2(1,10-phen)][PF6]) was conducted (Scheme 4). Surprisingly, despite the extended π-conjugation of phenanthroline compared to bpy, the product (12) showed no NIR transition (Figure 7A). This is in stark contrast to the enhanced NIR absorptions of 5. Furthermore, 12 exhibits significantly red-shifted visible light transitions compared to 2 – 11, affording a dark green solution (Figure 7B). Additionally, in contrast to the paramagnetic 2 – 11, 12 was EPR silent at room temperature (Figure 7C). Upon air exposure, however, the solution of 12 readily turned to an EPR-active red solution (Figure 7C). These properties of 12 were drastically different from the nature of 2 – 11, yet explained by its unexpected solid-state

structure (Figure 7D). Intriguingly, single-crystal X-ray diffraction studies disclosed that 12 is an apparent dimer as opposed to the anticipated monomer (12-monomer in Scheme 4). We hypothesize that 12 arises from a bimolecular C–C bond (1.584 Å) coupling between two of the reduced monomeric products, 12-monomer (Scheme 4). Upon C–C bond formation, the nascent L2-type phenanthroline ligand is dearomatized, serving as an XL-type donor for each metal center to afford a neutral Ir(III) dimeric species. Consequently, the initial radical character residing mostly on a phenanthroline ligand of 12-monomer is quenched, generating closed-shell, EPR silent complex 12. A similar C–C σ- bond formation was previously reported with a Cp*2Yb complex bearing a di-methyl substituted phenanthroline ligand.17   These notable features of 12 reflect the absence of radical character in its ground state, yet, we note that 12 is still highly air and moisture sensitive, similar to 2 – 11. These notable features of 12 re-emphasize that the previously mentioned properties of 2 – 11 can be attributed to their doublet, ligand-centered radical configuration.

2.6. Photoinduced ET reactivities of reduced Ir chromo-

phores.


<!-- Page 7 -->


The foregoing data demonstrate that the reduced Ir chromophores (2 – 11) absorb a wide range of light from UV to NIR. This observation suggests that not only the conventional Ir photocatalyst but also its singly-reduced form can absorb visible photons and thus, potentially participate in a photoinduced bimolecular ET (Figure 1A).4 Indeed, one recent study proposed that in situ generated 11 is capable of cleaving an aliphatic C–X (X = Cl, Br, I) bond via excited state ET.8 The study proposed that 11 can be generated upon photoirradiation from its cationic precursor [Ir(ppy)2(4,4’-dtBubpy)][PF6] using ascorbic acid as a

sacrificial electron donor. Additionally, the authors hypothesized that 11 could be stabilized via non-covalent interactions in aqueous micellar solutions.8 However, in our hands all of the reduced Ir chromophores (2 – 11) and the dimerized form of 12 are extremely air- and moisture sensitive. Exposure to air results in immediate decomposition as judged by 1H NMR spectroscopy accompanied by a color change to pale yellow.

Moreover, rapid degradation was observed in protic or coordinating solvents such as dichloromethane, tetrahydrofuran, diethyl ether, or acetonitrile. Particularly, isolated 11, which is the most electron-rich and the most reducing species among the series, fumed upon attempted dissolution in dichloromethane. Among the various solvents, isolated materials of 2 – 12 are stable in a degassed and dried hydrocarbon solvent such as benzene, toluene, and cyclohexane. In this regard, a similar observation on the instability of the reduced Ir intermediate (e.g., 11) towards a relatively acidic α-C–H bond of an oxidized sacrificial electron donor (e.g., NEt3+•) has previously been reported.18  Due to the limited chemical stability of these reduced Ir chromophores, we sought to investigate their photo-reactivity in a stoichiometric fashion using isolated material (e.g., 4 or 11). As discussed earlier, we envisioned that the excited state of the reduced Ir-chromophore (*PS•–) could be a viable partner for ET, specifically for challenging reductions such as the dehalogenation of aryl halides.19 To test this hypothesis, isolated 11 in benzene-d6 was treated with 1 equivalent of thoroughly degassed and dried bromobenzene under N2 atmosphere within an air-free J. Young tube (Figure 8A).

Gratifyingly, quantitative formation of biphenyl was detected upon purple or blue light (390 or 425 nm) irradiation (Figure 8A). Concomitantly, 11 was cleanly oxidized by one electron to afford the corresponding cationic complex possessing a bromide anion (13) (Figure 8B). Single-crystal Xray diffraction studies revealed that the 4,4’-d(tBu)bpy ligand of 13 exhibited C–H bond distances consistent with a neutral rather than an anionic bpy moiety. Furthermore, the solid-state structure of 13 revealed non-covalent association between C(3)–H bonds of the 4,4’- d(tBu)bpy ligand and bromide anion. The corresponding 1H resonance was shifted downfield compared to [Ir(ppy)2(4,4’- dtBubpy)][PF6], suggesting that this interaction is retained in solution (Figure 8C).20 When the same reaction was performed in the dark, neither 11 nor bromobenzene was consumed. These observations suggest that the dehalogenative C–C bond formation occurs via a photoinduced electron transfer directly from the singly-reduced Ir chromophore 11. However, the dehalogenation reactivity was absent following red/NIR irradiation, suggesting that high-energy photons are essential for the reductive dehalogenation. Such wavelength-dependent reactivity may suggest that rather than


<!-- Page 8 -->


the lowest-energy excited state of 11, another higher-energy excited state (e.g., metal-to-ligand charge transfer (d → ppy π*) state) would generate a viable excited state for the observed reactivity. This observation led us to examine the photophysical properties of the reduced Ir chromophores both at the 350 nm and 800 nm excitation.

2.7. Photophysical properties of reduced Ir chromo-

phores. To this end, ultrafast phenomena of isolated 2 – 11 upon photoirradiation were probed by femtosecond transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy. As noted in previous sections, owing to the limited chemical stability of reduced Ir chromophores, all samples were prepared in an air-free J. Young

cuvette using degassed anhydrous cyclohexane under N2 atmosphere and excited at 350 nm and 800 nm (Figure 4A and 9). As shown in Figure 9A, the TA difference spectrum of 4, for example, displays a negative absorption at 470 – 550 nm corresponding to the ground state bleach (GSB). Simultaneously, the emerging feature (∆A > 0) or the excited state absorption (ESA) of the excited 4 (e.g., (*PS•–) = 24*) was detected. Decay of the excited state required either two or three lifetimes to fit when pumped with 350 nm and 800 nm, respectively (Table S-3 and Table S-4). Akin to the other one-electron reduced photoredox catalysts (e.g., PDI, DCA, Acr, and NMI in Figure 1B), these lifetimes are short, with the largest approaching 20 ps (e.g., 2(PDI•–)*: τ = 160 ps, 2(NMI•–)*: τ = 24 ps). 7c, 21

*Figure 10. (A, B) Transient absorption difference spectra of 4 in the presence of chlorobenzene in degassed and dried cyclohexane upon 350 nm and (C) 800 nm pulsed laser excitation.*

This is a typical property for a doublet spin system. For both pump wavelengths, the first lifetime is assigned decay of the electronic excited state, i.e. D1 under 800 nm excitation or Dn under 350 nm excitation. The remaining lifetimes are then assigned as vibrational cooling of a hot ground state. A vibrationally hot ground state typically displays a spectrum with GSBs and ESAs immediately to the red, which matches the appearance of our spectra after ~5-7 ps.

Next, cyclohexane solutions of 2 – 11 were excited at 800 nm (Figure 9B) and the corresponding lifetime values were summarized in Table S-4. In all cases, similar to the lifetime values measured upon 350 nm excitation, picosecond lifetimes were observed. We note, however, that our attempts to measure the lifetime of 5 upon 800 nm excitation were not successful due to the unexpected sample degradation. Upon irradiation by a 800 nm pulsed laser, the initially homogenous cyclohexane solution of 5 rapidly became


<!-- Page 9 -->


heterogeneous. These observations suggest that types of the accessible excited states, and thus, the corresponding photo-reactivity could be distinct between the 350 and 800 nm excitations as shown by the additional ΔA > 0 features in Figure 9A. More in-depth photophysical studies will be necessary to explain the observed wavelength-dependent reactivity. Nevertheless, we indeed observed such wavelength-dependent reactivity between 4 and chlorobenzene via transient absorption spectroscopy (Figure 10). Upon photoexcitation with 350 nm pulsed-laser, new spectral features that resemble the non-reduced Ir complex appear after very short time delays and persist through the length of the experiment (Figure 10A and 10B). These results may indicate the irreversible formation of the corresponding cationic Ir complex akin to 13 (e.g., [Ir(dFCF3ppy)2(4,4’-dtBubpy)][Cl]) upon the excited state dehalogenation. In contrast, 800 nm excitation of 4 in the presence of chlorobenzene showed unchanged dynamics, in line with the observed wavelengthdependent reactivity (Figure 10C ). Collectively, given the short lifetime of (24*), the observed dehalogenation reactivity could be due to a relatively high concentration of the quencher under the stoichiometric conditions. Alternatively, pre-association of 4 with a quencher in their ground states could potentially enable ET in the excited state despite the short lifetime. While the measurement of the binding constant between 4 and fluorobenzene in a solution was unsuccessful, the titration experiments utilizing a UV/vis absorption spectroscopy exhibited perturbation in absorbance, consistent with a ground state interaction (Figure S-96). Additionally, we note that none of the reduced Ir compound (e.g., 2 – 11) shows the dehalogenation reactivity towards fluorobenzene under blue light. Therefore, we propose that the doublet excited state is not reducing enough to reduce fluorobenzene, but bromo- or chlorobenzene (-2.44 V and -2.58 V vs. SCE, respectively). More in-depth mechanistic studies on the reaction mechanism and photophysics are in progress. Nevertheless, these results suggests that not only the conventional Ir(III) photoredox catalyst (e.g., [IrIII(dFCF3ppy)2(4,4’- dtBubpy)][PF6]), but also its singly-reduced form can conceivably participate in a photoinduced bimolecular ET in multiphoton excitation processes. Indeed, a recent study has shown that the reduced PDI is still capable of undergoing bimolecular electron transfer at its excited state despite of its extremely short lifetime (e.g., 160 ps).21 These results demonstrate the direct involvement of a mono-reduced Ir-based chromophore during consecutive photoexcitation processes.4, 20 Recently, Wärnmark and coworkers have shown the direct isolation of a singly-reduced Fe-based photoredox catalyst and its viability as a second photon absorber for the Z-scheme like two-photon processes.10 Thus far, in order to study the involvement of a singly-reduced chromophore during photoredox catalysis, a two-photon laser setup was required; (1) the first photon generates the target species in situ and (2) the second photon for its subsequent excitation. In this regard, we believe that our synthetic route enabling the isolation of the reduced chromophore will provide opportunities to better establish the nature of the second excited state using more accessible transient spectroscopies. Ongoing work aims to

further characterize the electronic structure and redox potential of this photoexcited state to broaden the scope of accessible chemical transformations using the reduced Ir chromophore. CONCLUSIONS One-electron reduced photosensitizers are crucial intermediates in photoredox catalysis. The independent synthesis and isolation of these reduced intermediates allowed us to study their physical and electronic structure. The doublet ground state electronic configuration was consistent across 11 different analogous Ir chromophores (e.g., 2 – 11) upon modifying substituents on either the bpy or ppy ligand. We are hopeful that these studies will provide useful characterization data for the reductively-quenched Ir photoredox catalysts both in their ground and excited states. Furthermore, this study will provide opportunities to examine mechanisms where a singly-reduced Ir chromophore is invoked as an intermediate. Future work will focus on studying the kinetics of the observed photoinduced bimolecular electron transfer mediated by the singly-reduced iridium chromophore and estimating the redox potentials of the corresponding excited state.
